19976-the-mabinogion-vol-3:
Lady Charlotte Guest translated The Mabinogion from medieval Welsh. Volume three is credited to her directly in this edition. It opens with Pwyll, prince of Dyved, lord of its seven cantrevs. Pwyll is at Narberth, his chief palace, one famous day. He is minded to go hunting in Glyn Cuch. That hunt begins the First Branch of the Mabinogi. Its wonders include a stolen child and a lady on a white horse.

Guest's eleven tales made Welsh literature world property. Pwyll's branch sets the pattern: courtesy, magic, and slow justice. Rhiannon, the lady of the hunt, dominates its memory. The translation's Victorian grace can soften the Welsh edge. Still, the strangeness survives triumphantly. Volume three holds the cycle's heart.
20828-traditions-of-the-north-american-i:
Verse of deer in battle and moose in race opens volume three of the Indian traditions. Panthers, lakes, and a white canoe crowd the lines with wild images. Woe waits the red man cast by fate in a midnight swamp, the poem warns.

Poems and tales close James Athearn Jones's three-volume set of native lore. Songs of war, love, and spirits round out the camp-fire store. The set aimed to save a fading oral world for print readers. Modern readers must sift its period flaws, yet its pages still hold early, earnest records of stories that tribes prized and passed down.
21262-the-works-of-christopher-marlowe-v:
A. H. Bullen's three-volume edition of Christopher Marlowe closes with this third volume, published in London in 1885. It gathers Marlowe's poems rather than his plays: Hero and Leander first, then his translations of Ovid's Elegies and the first book of Lucan. The Passionate Shepherd to His Love, the lyric everyone knows, stands near the end.

Epigrams by John Davies, fragments, and a dialogue in verse fill out the volume, with appendices and an index to the notes. Two editions of Hero and Leander appeared in 1598, one with only Marlowe's part. Bullen's edition helped fix Marlowe's standing as a poet beside his fame as a dramatist.
21811-the-works-of-lord-byron-vol-3:
Lord Byron's narrative poems fill this third volume of his works, in an edition rich with notes by editor E. H. Coleridge. The Giaour and The Bride of Abydos stand among the poems here, tales of the Levant that made Byron famous across Europe. Coleridge prints deleted lines and variant readings from Byron's own manuscripts. Byron's footnotes stand beside the editor's, marked so readers can tell them apart.

These poems mix romance, guilt, and wild eastern scenery in Byron's swift, glowing verse. They were the sensation of their years, and their heroes gave English the word Byronic. The heavy notes suit the volume to study as well as pleasure. It is Byron with his workshop doors open, drafts and all.
22591-a-political-history-of-the-state-o:
A Political History of the State of New York is a three-volume history issued by Henry Holt and Company in 1906. The catalog record credits the publisher rather than a personal author. New York's politics, from colonial days onward, shaped the nation far beyond the state's borders, and this work traces that story in detail.

The sample opens at the birth of the state, as the second Continental Congress in May 1776 urged colonies without sound governments to form new ones fit for war. New York's patriot government, the writer notes, had not wholly satisfied its people. From that shaky start the volumes follow parties, leaders, and elections. Students of American political history will find a full period account of the Empire State's public life.
a-book-of-old-ballads-volume-3: The third volume of Nichols' old ballads — more border raids, tragic loves, and merry outlaws — continues his spirited collection. His retellings keep the minstrel spirit alive for new ears. Balladry's best, in its third gathering. Outlaws and lovers ride again through his rousing pages.
a-connecticut-yankee-in-king-arthur-s-co: Hank's reforms — schools, newspapers, and soap — advance in this third part, to Merlin's dismay. Twain's satire of chivalry and church sharpens. The Yankee's Connecticut energy transforms Camelot. Soap, schools, and secret factories undermine the age of chivalry. Every new gadget strikes another blow for common sense over superstition.
a-far-country-volume-3: The third volume brings A Far Country toward its powerful close. The full costs of ambition come due for the driven hero. Love and conscience demand their long-delayed reckoning. The sweeping novel reaches a fitting end.
a-hazard-of-new-fortunes-volume-3: Howells's Hazard of New Fortunes, volume three: the middle act. New York's literary life. The dean's great novel. Realism at its best, howells's middle act, new York literary life, realism at its best, Howells's novel.
a-history-of-science-volume-3: Henry Smith Williams's third volume of popular science history covers the great awakening: Copernicus, Galileo, Newton, and the birth of modern method. Accessible and wide-ranging, it brings the scientific revolution to life for general readers. Knowledge made readable and exciting.
a-life-for-a-life-volume-1-of-3: A Life for a Life, volume one of three, by Dinah Craik. The tale begins. This book preserves that novel. History keeps its place secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. Readers can find it here.
a-woodland-queen-reine-des-bois-volume-3: The third volume of A Woodland Queen brings the rural tale home. The brave heroine's fate is sealed among the woods she loves. Theuriet's nature poetry shines on every page. A gentle and fragrant close to the story.
ancient-records-egypt-breasted-1906-vol-:
Breasted's third volume of Ancient Records, published in 1906, covers the nineteenth dynasty. Seti I and Ramesses II dominate its pages: campaigns in Asia, the great battle of Kadesh, and the peace treaty with the Hittites that followed. Temple inscriptions at Karnak and Abu Simbel supply many of the texts in Breasted's translation.

The Kadesh poems and the treaty text rank among the most studied documents of the ancient world. Later records in the volume trace the dynasty's slow strain under invasion and internal dispute. Breasted arranges all of it with dates, sources, and sober notes. Volume three gives the Ramesside age its full documentary weight. Egypt's voice here is proud, detailed, and increasingly defensive.
ante-nicene-fathers-vol-3:
Tertullian fills volume three of the Ante-Nicene Fathers, the 1885 set edited by Alexander Roberts and James Donaldson. Tertullian of Carthage, writing around 200 AD, was the founder of Latin Christianity's voice. No early writer is fiercer, funnier, or more quotable.

His apologetic works answer pagan slanders and demand fair treatment for Christians before the law. Other treatises rule on prayer, dress, idolatry, and the games, with a rigor that spares no one. Tertullian coined much of the Latin vocabulary of theology, including the word for Trinity. The volume gives the whole of his surviving early work in English dress.
arabian-nights-lane-1877-vol-3:
Volume III of Lane's Thousand and One Nights, in the 1877 printing, completes his pioneering scholarly version. Edward William Lane first issued the work from 1838 to 1840, with drawings and notes drawn from his years in Egypt. The final volume carries Shahrazad's tales to their close in his measured English.

Lane's set taught Victorian Britain to take the Nights seriously as literature and as evidence of Arab life. His omissions are famous, but so is his fidelity where he does translate. Volume III rounds out a version that stands beside Payne's and Burton's as one of the three great English Nights.
arabian-nights-payne-1882-vol-3:
Volume III of Payne's Thousand Nights and One Night, dated 1882, carries the Calcutta text forward in English. The tales turn and turn again: voyages, transformations, and lovers parted by fate and reunited by wit. John Payne's rendering stays complete and unexpurgated, the quality that made his the first full English Nights.

Between Burton's ornate version and Lane's trimmed one, Payne's stands as the full record for its age. Readers who follow the sequence feel the great story-cycle breathing at its own slow, hypnotic pace. Volume III holds the middle of the early nights, with six volumes still to come.
aristophanes-plays-rogers-loeb-1924-vol-:
The third Rogers volume of Aristophanes, published in 1924, completes the Loeb set with Lysistrata, the Thesmophoriazusae, the Ecclesiazusae, and Plutus. In Lysistrata the women of Greece end a war by refusing their husbands until peace is made. Its fame has only grown with the centuries.

The Thesmophoriazusae traps a spy inside a women's festival, mocked in Euripides' own style. The Ecclesiazusae hands Athens to its women, who decree shared property and shared spouses. Plutus, the last play, restores the god of wealth's sight and upends rich and poor. Rogers's rhymes carry the bawdy, topical energy across twenty-four centuries. With this volume the eleven surviving comedies stand complete.
arnold-history-rome-vol-3:
Crisis grips Rome in the third volume of Arnold's History of Rome, from 1838. The Gracchi seek reform, Marius and Sulla march armies on the city, and the free state totters. Arnold, a liberal Englishman, watched ancient liberty die with a keen, wary eye.

He treats the late Republic as a warning for any free people. Wealth, faction, and armed ambition rot the laws from within. Each reform missed makes the next blow worse. His account gains urgency from that parallel, and the volume closes his history with a somber lesson on how republics fall when citizens cease to guard them.
athenaeus-deipnosophists-yonge-vol-3:
Volume three completes Yonge's translation of Athenaeus's Deipnosophists. The banquet of the learned reaches its last courses in this volume. Each dish still sets off cascades of quotation from vanished books.

Slaves, drinking customs, and famous courtesans occupy the later talk. Athenaeus's guests display learning as a competitive sport to the end. The whole work preserves fragments of hundreds of lost Greek writers. Historians of food, music, and daily life mine it constantly. Yonge's three volumes gave English readers the complete ancient feast. Chatty and enormous, the Deipnosophists remains a quarry no classicist can ignore for long.
b09-zwingli-latin-works-3:
The third volume of the Latin Works and Correspondence of Huldreich Zwingli covers 1528 to 1531. Clarence Nevin Heller edited the volume, with introductions by George Warren Richards, in the 1929 Philadelphia issue. The translators of the earlier Jackson edition rendered the Latin texts into English.

Zwingli's last years were his hardest: dispute with Luther over the Lord's Supper, and war clouds over the Swiss cantons. He died in battle at Kappel in 1531, and the correspondence runs to that end. These pages show a reformer holding a city, a pulpit, and a cause at once. The volume completes the standard English record of his Latin works.
babylonian-talmud-rodkinson-vol-3:
Volume three of Michael L. Rodkinson's English Babylonian Talmud holds Tract Erubin, the laws of Sabbath boundaries. Erubin rules seem narrow, but they shape how a whole town keeps the Sabbath together. The 1918 edition continues Rodkinson's twenty-volume translation, the first full English Talmud.

An erub is a shared boundary that lets people carry in public space as if it were one yard. The tractate works out how such boundaries are made: walls, wires, shared food, and joined courtyards. Disputes run over every detail, from a ditch to a leaky wall. The volume shows the rabbis' genius for building community by law.
badauni-muntakhab-vol-3:
Scholars, saints, and poets crowd the third volume of Badauni's Muntakhab, in T. W. Haig's 1899 English version. Rather than battles and decrees, this book offers lives. It forms a kind of who's who of the mind in Akbar's India.

Brief lives trace teachers, mystics, calligraphers, and verse makers of the age. Badauni judges each man by his faith, learning, and character. Praise and blame fall in his usual tart measure. For readers of Mughal culture, the volume is gold: a portrait gallery of a golden age, drawn by a man who knew many of its sitters.
bancroft-history-us-vol-3:
Wars with France shake the colonies in the third volume of Bancroft's History, from 1856. Colonial rights are asserted more boldly as the stakes grow higher each year. The road bends, year by year, toward revolt against Britain.

Bancroft builds his case that liberty was America's birthright from the start. Frontier fights and imperial policy grind against each other in his pages. Assemblies learn to say no, and to mean it. He writes with rising drama here. The stage is set for the crisis volumes that follow in his vast narrative of a people becoming a nation.
byron-letters-vol-3:
Volume Three of Byron's Letters and Journals, in Prothero's 1898 edition, covers his final years. Byron settled in Italy, wrote his greatest poems, and grew restless for action. The Greek war for independence gave him a cause at last.

The letters trace his life with the Shelleys, the feuds of the Italian years, and the writing of Don Juan. Then comes his sailing for Greece in 1823 to aid the rebels. He died at Missolonghi in 1824, aged thirty-six. This closing volume completes the standard record of Byron's life in his own brilliant words. Prothero closes the set with a full index to all three volumes.
carlyle-cromwell-letters-vol-3:
The Protectorate closes Carlyle's Cromwell in this third volume of the 1904 Lomas edition. Cromwell rules England without a king, facing parliaments, plots, and his own failing health. His death in 1658 ends both the book and an era.

Letters and speeches show triumph turning to loneliness and strain. The great Puritan governs, exhorts, and mourns in his own stark words. Carlyle's devotion to his hero never wavers to the last page. The full set stands as a founding act of Cromwell scholarship. It lets a maligned ruler argue his own case before posterity at last, in full.
carlyle-friedrich-vol-3:
Frederick faces a ring of foes in the third volume of Carlyle's history, in the 1884 printing. The Seven Years' War begins, and Prussia stands against Austria, France, and Russia at once. Defeat stalks the king through his darkest campaigns.

Carlyle tells of endurance raised to the level of tragedy. The great king's genius and grit hold a small state together. Battles turn on hours, and hope on rumor and weather. His devoted English champion spares no detail of the strain. The volume shows hero-worship at its most intense, wedded to research of staggering depth and labor.

Burney's great novel ends as it lived: with wit, feeling, and moral grace. A satisfying finale. Delirium, devotion, and a hard-won happy ending crown one of the age's finest novels.

cicero-letters-shuckburgh-vol-3:
Civil war between Caesar and Pompey fills the third volume of Cicero's letters, in Shuckburgh's 1899 version. The great orator is caught between two giants. He writes in anguish to friends as Rome tears itself apart.

Each letter weighs flight, loyalty, safety, and shame anew. Cicero's brilliance and worry stand bare on every page. He knows the Republic he loves is dying either way. The volume gives history in its raw state. Outcomes have not yet hardened into fate, and a gifted man tries, letter by letter, to keep his honor intact. Few sources let a reader watch a republic die so closely.
cinq-mars-volume-3: The third volume of Cinq-Mars deepens the bold conspiracy. The young and daring favorite plots against the all-powerful cardinal. Danger mounts steadily with every turning page. Vigny's romantic history told at full power.
curtius-history-greece-vol-3:
Persia invades in the third volume of Curtius's History of Greece, in Ward's 1868 version. Marathon, Thermopylae, and Salamis form its blazing core. Small Greek cities face the might of the Persian Empire and win.

Curtius tells the heroic age with a scholar's care and a poet's pulse. Leonidas falls, Themistocles schemes, and free men outfight a host. The stakes, he insists, were the future of the West itself. Readers get the full sweep of the wars that saved Greek freedom. A master tells the tale, one who knew the ground and the sources well. His love for Greece glows on every page of the wars.
dialogues-of-the-buddha-vol-3:
The third volume of the Dialogues of the Buddha, from 1921, completes the Rhys Davids translation of the Digha Nikaya. T. W. Rhys Davids died the next year; his wife Caroline carried the Pali Text Society's work onward. The final long discourses of the collection stand here.

Late suttas take up the marks of a great man, the chanting of the teaching in council, and the Buddha's instructions for the order after his death. One discourse lists the points of doctrine in numbered sets, built for memory and recital. Read across three volumes, the Digha gives the fullest picture of the Buddha as a teacher among rivals. The set remains a standard English Nikaya.
dio-cassius-roman-history-cary-vol-3:
With books thirty-six through forty, the Roman History of Dio Cassius starts to survive in full, not just in scraps. Earnest Cary's Loeb translation fills this third volume. Dio wrote around 230 CE, and from here his story of the late republic runs without large gaps.

Pompey rises on his eastern victories, and Catiline plots against the state. Caesar then marches through Gaul while the senate and the great men pull Rome toward civil war. Dio tells these years with a senator's eye for power and pride. The volume lands the reader at the edge of the war that ended the republic.
dionysius-halicarnassus-roman-antiquitie:
Edward Spelman's 1758 translation of Dionysius of Halicarnassus reaches books six through eight in this third volume. The Roman Antiquities, written around 7 BCE, now covers the hard early years of the republic. Debt, hunger, and pride set the orders of Rome at odds.

The struggle of the orders fills these books: plebeians walk out of the city, tribunes rise to guard them, and war with the Volscians presses from outside. Coriolanus, exiled and turned enemy, marches on Rome and is turned back by his mother. Dionysius gives the fullest surviving tale of these fights. His speeches show how Greeks of his age read Roman virtue.
droll-stories-volume-3: Volume three of Balzac's Droll Stories: the last of the bawdy tales of old France. Rabelaisian to the end, they complete the feast. The master's earthiest work, concluded. Balzac's last laugh is his broadest, the feast ends with a Rabelaisian roar.
ethics-part-3: Part 3 of Spinoza's Ethics is his famous study of the emotions: love, hate, hope, fear, and forty more, each defined and traced to its causes. Spinoza treats feelings like geometry, mapping how they control us. Revolutionary in its cool analysis, it remains one of the deepest accounts of human passion ever written.
euclid-elements-heath-vol-3:
Heath's third Euclid volume covers Books Ten through Thirteen, completing the Elements. The 1908 edition closes with geometry's most demanding ancient material. Book Ten alone classifies irrational lengths at enormous length.

That classification was antiquity's hardest mathematics, filling a quarter of the whole work. Books Eleven through Thirteen turn to solid geometry and its figures. The five Platonic solids close the Elements in a famous finale. Euclid proves that exactly five regular solids can exist. Geometry here climbs into philosophy's own country, as Plato had hoped. Heath's notes guide readers through the densest proofs with patience.
euripides-plays-way-loeb-1912-vol-3:
Way's third Loeb volume of Euripides, first printed in 1912, holds the Bacchanals, the Madness of Hercules, the Children of Hercules, the Phoenician Maidens, and the Suppliants. The scan staged here is a 1930 reprint of the edition. The Bacchae, often ranked Euripides' greatest play, stands first here.

In it the god Dionysus returns to Thebes and drives its king to a gruesome death. Hercules, struck mad by Hera, kills his own wife and children in his hall. The remaining plays plead for Athens as protector of the weak and the dead. Way's complete verse set lets readers follow Euripides' darkening view of gods and war. No other English Euripides of the age attempted all nineteen plays.
freeman-norman-conquest-vol-3:
Conquest turns brutal in the third volume of Freeman's History, from 1867, covering the years 1066 to 1070. William subdues the north in the harrying, a winter of fire and famine. Castles rise to lock down a sullen, broken land.

Freeman spares nothing in telling conquest as catastrophe. Rebellions flare and are crushed with methodical cruelty. His thoroughness as a scholar matches his passion as a partisan. The volume shows what invasion really cost ordinary folk. Pageants of kings often skip that side of 1066. It is the darkest book of his great set, and among the most powerful.
froude-english-ireland-vol-3:
Rebellion and Union close Froude's Irish history in this third volume, from 1872. Wolfe Tone's rising of 1798 fails in blood and reprisal. The Act of Union then folds Ireland's parliament into Westminster's for good.

Froude calls these years the tragic end of Ireland's darkest century. French fleets, pike charges, and scaffold speeches crowd his climax. His account was controversial then and remains so now. Few histories of the period match its narrative power, whatever readers make of its verdicts. The volume completes a trilogy that still shapes debate on England's rule in Ireland today. Its force explains why Irish readers still argue with it fiercely.
froude-history-england-vol-3:
Later Henrician years fill the third volume of Froude's History, in the 1870 printing. Thomas Cromwell falls from power and goes to his death. The king's six wives meet their varied, often tragic fates as his rule hardens into tyranny.

Froude does not flinch from his hero's dark side in this book. Executions, forced oaths, and fear mark the court he describes. Yet he still defends the Reformation as a needful break with Rome. The volume shows Tudor power at its most ruthless, and it tests the reader's sympathy for both the king and the cause he served.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-3:
Combined Chiefs of Staff minutes for July 16, 1945, record the Allied military chiefs' afternoon session at Potsdam. The top secret record is an unnumbered item following document 710 in volume two. Much of it turns on the wording of surrender terms for Japan.

After approving the conference program paper, the chiefs took up an estimate of the enemy situation. Sir Alan Brooke pointed to a line in it touching the survival of Japan's imperial institution. He asked if the U.S. chiefs had weighed how to interpret unconditional surrender for the Japanese. From a military view, he argued, explaining the term could shorten the war in outlying areas. If the throne survived, the Emperor could order far-flung garrisons to cease fire. If the dynasty were destroyed, those garrisons might fight on for months or years.
