gellius-attic-nights-rolfe-loeb-vol-3:
The Attic Nights of Aulus Gellius closes with books fourteen through twenty in this third Loeb volume, translated by John C. Rolfe. Gellius wrote his notebook of Roman lore in the second century, for his children and for readers like them. The last books bring the twenty-book miscellany to its end.

Star lore, old laws, word histories, and tales of philosophers fill these pages. Gellius keeps quoting lost authors, and each quote is a small rescue from oblivion. His own voice stays modest and eager, a friend showing you his shelves. The full set preserves more lost Latin prose than any other single book of its age.
hallam-constitutional-history-vol-3:
Restoration to George the Second fills the third volume of Hallam's Constitutional History, from 1827. The Glorious Revolution expels James the Second and settles the crown by law. The Bill of Rights then fixes limits that kings must not cross.

Hallam completes his great argument in this closing book. England's constitution appears as the slow triumph of law over arbitrary power. Parties, parliaments, and courts settle into their modern shapes here. His judgments shaped a century of political thought and debate. The full work remains a founding text of Whig history, prized for learning, balance, and quiet moral force.
hallam-middle-ages-vol-3:
Towns, trade, and learning close Hallam's medieval survey in this third volume, from 1860. Cities grow rich and free as feudal bonds loosen across Europe. Schools revive old learning, and the first light of a new age appears on many horizons.

Hallam ends his great work where the modern world begins. He traces the institutions that would shape all that followed after. Commerce, law, and letters rise together in his final chapters. The three volumes form a pioneering survey in English. They taught their century to see the Middle Ages as the seedbed of modern Europe, not its dark prelude.
hawkesworth-account-voyages-southern-hem:
The third volume of Hawkesworth's Account of the Voyages, from 1773, closes the official set. It carries Cook's first voyage in the Endeavour to its end: the charting of New Zealand, the east coast of Australia, and the wreck on the Great Barrier Reef. It also looks ahead to Cook's second voyage, then fitting out.

The Endeavour's near-loss on the reef, and her crew's fight to save her, makes gripping reading. Botany Bay, named for Banks's plants, enters the map here. Hawkesworth's smooth first-person blend of Cook's and Banks's journals drew fire for liberties taken. Even so, the three volumes fixed the Pacific in Europe's imagination.
history-of-the-decline-and-fall-of-the-r: The middle volumes of Gibbon's masterpiece carry the story through the fall of Rome itself: barbarian invasions, the sack of the city, and the long agony of the Western Empire. Gibbon's cool judgment and rolling sentences make catastrophe read like epic. Volume by volume, the greatest history in English builds toward its devastating climax.
humboldt-cosmos-otte-vol-3:
The third volume of Humboldt's Cosmos, in Otté's English translation, returns to the heavens with the tools of mature astronomy. Humboldt planned the work as a physical description of the universe, and this volume treats the celestial half in depth. It followed volumes one and two in the Bohn edition of 1849.

Stars, double stars, nebulae, and the solar system's planets and comets pass in ordered review. Humboldt weighs what the telescope had proven by mid-century and marks the open questions plainly. His care to separate fact from guess made Cosmos a model of honest popular science. The volume also holds his thoughts on the light and heat of the sun.
humboldt-personal-narrative-williams-vol:
The third volume of Humboldt's Personal Narrative, in Williams's translation, came out in 1818. It carries the expedition down its boldest line: the Orinoco river system. Humboldt set out to prove the Orinoco joins the Amazon through the Casiquiare canal, a link geographers doubted.

By canoe, through clouds of biting insects, the party runs rapids and portages into the Rio Negro. Humboldt confirms the canal with his own instruments, redrawing the map of a continent. He records missions, river peoples, and the poisons and medicines of the forest. The volume is the heart of the whole Narrative, where his fame as an explorer was made.
ibsen-collected-works-archer-vol-3:
Brand preaches all or nothing, and the demand slowly destroys everyone he loves. Ibsen's towering verse drama fills the third volume of Archer's English edition, in C. H. Herford's translation, published in 1908. A young priest in a mountain parish refuses every compromise the world offers him.

The play became a sensation across Scandinavia, argued over in pulpits and newspapers alike. Brand's purity inspires and horrifies in equal measure, which is the tragedy's engine. Is he a saint of integrity or a fanatic drunk on his own will? Ibsen never answers cleanly. The work stands as his most uncompromising statement, a tragedy of idealism itself.
ihne-history-rome-vol-3:
Carthage and Rome collide in the third volume of Ihne's History, from 1871. Hannibal crosses the Alps and wins at Cannae, Rome's darkest day of the age. Scipio answers by carrying the war to Africa itself and ending it at Zama.

Ihne tells the titanic struggle with clarity and gripping pace. Two great republics fight for mastery of the western Mediterranean world. His chapters balance strategy, politics, and the temper of each people. Few accounts of the Punic Wars match its order and force. The volume stands among the clearest ever written on the war that made Rome a world power.
isbe-1915-vol-3:
Volume 3 of Orr's International Standard Bible Encyclopedia came out in 1915 with the rest of the set. The encyclopedia aimed to give Bible readers a complete reference that joined sound scholarship to traditional faith. By the third volume, the undertaking was in mid-course, the alphabet well advanced.

More of the ancient world is recovered here, and more of Scripture's background explained, article by signed article. The steady, learned progress of Orr's project shows on every page: maps, lists, and long treatments of major topics beside short notes on small names. The set became the standard Bible dictionary of its age for conservative readers. Volume 3 keeps the standard through the middle of the alphabet, and students of the period still consult it for the state of knowledge in 1915.
jack-sheppard-a-romance-vol-1-of-3: Jack Sheppard, a romance, volume one of three, by Ainsworth. The tale begins. This book preserves that novel. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
jack-sheppard-a-romance-vol-2-of-3: Jack Sheppard, a romance, volume two of three, by Ainsworth. The middle of the tale. This book preserves that novel. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
jack-sheppard-a-romance-vol-3-of-3: Jack Sheppard, a romance, volume three of three, by Ainsworth. The tale concludes. This book preserves that novel. Future scholars will discover it. It retains its place in time. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
jataka-cowell-vol-3:
The third volume of Cowell's Jataka came out in 1897, midway in the six-volume English set. H. T. Francis and R. A. Neil were among the translators from the Pali under E. B. Cowell's editorship. The tales continue in their fixed order, birth after birth.

Here the future Buddha appears in longer, richer stories, some running to small novellas of courts and quests. Tricksters test him, kings misjudge him, and his past wisdom unties each knot. The morals stay plain: generosity over grasping, calm over rage, truth over gain. Scholars mine the Jataka for early Indian life; general readers simply enjoy the tales. Volume three holds some of the best.
john-lothrop-motley-a-memoir-volume-3:
Volume three of Oliver Wendell Holmes's memoir of John Lothrop Motley reaches the historian's last work. Chapter twenty-two opens in 1874, when Motley was sixty. His final book was The Life and Death of John of Barneveld, with a view of the causes of the Thirty Years' War. Holmes calls it a history rather than a biography.

The Barneveld book forms an interlude in Motley's grand plan, the Eighty Years' Tragedy of Dutch freedom. Its last act, on the Thirty Years' War, was never written. British reviews praised the book as a worthy match for his earlier volumes. Holmes quotes the London Quarterly calling the whole series a fine, continuous story. This volume carries the memoir toward the end of Motley's laboring life.
john-marchmont-s-legacy-volume-1-of-3:
Volume one of John Marchmont's Legacy is a sensation novel by M. E. Braddon, author of Lady Audley's Secret. The third edition was published by Tinsley Brothers of London in 1863. Braddon dedicates the story to her mother. Fourteen chapters make up this first volume, from The Man with the Banner to Driven Away.

The titles name the people and the stakes: Little Mary, the Lincolnshire property, and Marchmont Towers. A young soldier returns, Olivia enters, and Mary's stepmother follows. Chapters of despair and desolation darken the middle of the volume. A figure called Paul appears before the close. This opening volume sets an inheritance tale of family pressure, love, and loss in motion.
john-marchmont-s-legacy-volume-2-of-3:
Volume two of John Marchmont's Legacy continues M. E. Braddon's sensation novel of 1863. Fourteen chapters carry the middle of the story, opening with Mary's Letter. Edward Arundel, Mrs. Marchmont, and Paul's sister move the plot forward. A stolen honeymoon and a figure risen from the grave raise the stakes.

Later chapters turn on a painting-room by the river and a paragraph in a newspaper. Edward's despair deepens, and one more sacrifice is demanded of the characters. The volume ends with a child's voice in the pavilion by the water. Braddon keeps the inheritance plot tightening, secret by secret, toward the final volume.
john-marchmont-s-legacy-volume-3-of-3:
Volume three of John Marchmont's Legacy closes M. E. Braddon's three-volume novel of 1863. It opens with Captain Arundel's Revenge, as Edward Arundel quits Lincolnshire for good. Fourteen chapters and an epilogue finish the tale. Titles promise deserted chambers, a widower's proposal, and the turning of the tide.

Belinda's wedding day and Mary's own story arrive late in the volume. The final chapter is named for the memory of wedded lives, and an epilogue follows. Edward leaves the neighborhood of Lawford Grange with a settled purpose at the start. From there Braddon resolves the legacy plot of love, money, and family claims that drove the earlier volumes.
john-marchmont-s-legacy-volumes-1-3:
John Marchmont's Legacy, in this combined edition, gathers all three volumes of M. E. Braddon's novel of 1863. Braddon, the author of Lady Audley's Secret, dedicates the story to her mother. The Tinsley Brothers third edition supplies the text. Volume one opens with The Man with the Banner and the chapter on little Mary.

The contents trace the whole arc: the Lincolnshire property, Marchmont Towers, and a young soldier's return. Olivia, Mary's stepmother, and a day of desolation follow in the first volume. Two more volumes carry the inheritance story through despair, return, and resolution. Readers get the complete sensation novel in one file, from the first banner to the epilogue.
joshua-volume-3:
Volume three of Georg Ebers's Joshua opens at chapter fifteen, beneath a sycamore tree. Miriam lies moaning while Hosea, the warrior she loves, paces in impatience. Something has suddenly towered like a mountain between them. Hosea bears promises that seem to him a merciful gift from the Most High, meant to lead his people to a fairer future.

Miriam fears he has come with terms like Uri's, a mediation her father and Moses reject. Her passion cools as she questions why he lingered and why he came without Ephraim. Ebers stages the scene under a clear, starry sky. Love and calling pull the two apart in one long, anxious night talk.
journeys-through-bookland-vol-3:
Volume three of Charles H. Sylvester's Journeys Through Bookland continues his reading plan for children, in the new edition of 1922. Lewis Carroll appears three times in the contents: The Mock Turtle's Story, Queen Alice, and The Walrus and the Carpenter. Mary Howitt's The Spider and the Fly stands beside them.

The volume also prints pieces of Robinson Crusoe and The Swiss Family Robinson. Thomas Hood's Faithless Sally Brown and William Dimond's The Mariner's Dream add verse. Aladdin and his wonderful lamp come from the Arabian Nights. A leprechaun tale by William Allingham and Beth Gelert's sad ballad widen the mix. Sylvester's set fed young readers the classics in pieces sized for them.
king-henry-vi-part-3:
An alarum opens Shakespeare's King Henry VI, Part 3, whose fuller title names the death of the Duke of York. Soldiers enter with Plantagenet's party after the sound of battle. Warwick, Edward, Richard, Norfolk, and Montague come on with him. Warwick asks at once how the King escaped their hands.

Plantagenet explains that they pursued the horsemen of the north too far. The King stole away slyly and left his men behind. Northumberland then cheered up the drooping army himself, Plantagenet says. Lord Clifford and Lord Stafford charged their main battle front abreast. The break-in puts the new fight in motion from the start.
l-abbe-constantin-volume-3:
Ludovic Halevy's novel of Longueval closes in this third volume of the English translation, which opens at chapter seven, titled Confidences. Jean Reynaud, godson of the Abbé Constantin, is now a welcome guest at the castle, where two rich young women have taken up residence. His friend Count Paul de Lavardens burns to be presented to them and teases Jean for the march he has already stolen.

Paul dreams openly of marrying Bettina and of the wealth that would come with her, while Jean hides behind his modest place as the curé's godson and the ladies' guide. The talk stays light, but money, rank, and love pull against each other in every visit. Readers who followed the sale of Longueval in the first volume here reach the story's end. The book closes on short, rueful maxims about love and quiet lives.
layamon-brut-madden-vol-3:
The third volume of Madden's 1847 edition of Layamon's Brut completes the chronicle. Layamon's verse history of Britain, written around 1200, ends with the last British king. After Arthur's fall, the poem follows the shrinking British kingdoms against the rising Saxons.

King succeeds king in brief, somber reigns until Cadwalader, the last, leaves for Rome and dies there in 689. The Britons' rule of the island ends, and the English age begins. Madden's facing translation makes the hard Middle English plain. The Brut as a whole is the first great English poem after the conquest, and its close is elegy.
lecky-england-18th-vol-3:
World war and the elder Pitt fill the third volume of Lecky's history, from 1890. The Seven Years' War spreads from Silesia to Canada and India. Britain rises toward world power on victories by land and sea across three continents.

Lecky writes at his most magisterial in these imperial chapters. He weighs strategy beside finance, and character beside chance, with calm authority. Pitt's energy drives the tale, yet the cost in debt and blood is never hidden. The volume forms a core part of his great work, showing how an island kingdom became, within one generation, the center of a worldwide empire.
lesage-gil-blas-smollett-1749-vol-3:
Volume 3 of Smollett's Gil Blas, dated 1749 in this set, completes Lesage's picaresque tale in English. Gil Blas, older now, has served many masters and seen courts and prisons from inside. The final volume brings his long education in the world to its close.

Gil rises to favor with powerful men, tastes the risks of court life, and at last withdraws to a quieter end. Lesage closed his hero's story with reflection rather than triumph, a rare note in rogue fiction. Smollett's translation, a landmark of 1749, made the whole tale part of English reading. The three volumes together chart a society through one servant's eyes.
life-and-letters-of-thomas-henry-huxley-:
The third volume of Huxley's letters covers 1887 to 1895. Leonard Huxley closes his father's story with these final years. A portrait from an 1890 photograph by Downey fronts the volume. Fifteen chapters divide the correspondence of the closing period.

Readers follow Huxley through his last controversies and honors. The letters slow in pace but keep his direct, honest tone. His interest in human problems outlasted his laboratory years. Together, the three volumes form the standard life of Darwin's bulldog. McQueen printed the Downey portrait of 1890 for this volume. The final chapter carries the correspondence into 1895.
life-on-the-mississippi-part-3:
Part Three opens as the river rises in Chapter 11. Small craft become a nuisance in chute after chute. Broad-horns block cramped places and shoal water at chute heads. Profane cordialities fly between crews at every meeting.

Fog brings sudden yells, tin pans, and looming log rafts. Crews snatch engine bells and pile on steam to escape. Steamboat clerks, Twain claims, carried assortments of religious tracts. Twenty times daily they cramped around bars behind drifting small-fry. Clerks carried the tracts twenty times a day, he insists. Broad-horns waited in the worst locality, the chute's head.
littre-dictionary-1863-vol-3:
Volume 3 of Littré's Dictionary carried the work through the heart of the alphabet. The dictionary had been appearing since 1863, and Littré, aging and often ill, drove it forward without lowering his standard. His method never changed: history first, with evidence for every sense.

The middle volumes hold some of the richest words in French. Littré gives each its genealogy, its old spellings, and its shifts of meaning across the centuries. Quotations from poets, chroniclers, and scientists crowd the pages. The great work's middle march shows no flagging, course by course of the crown of French lexicography. Scholars still cite Littré where later dictionaries are silent, above all for older French. Volume 3 is the project at its fullest stretch, the language's biography at its widest point.
lord-ormont-and-his-aminta-volume-3:
Volume 3 carries George Meredith's Lord Ormont and His Aminta into Book 3. It opens at a dinner at Mrs. Lawrence's house, where a Horse Guards orderly brings a large parcel. Lord Ormont keeps the company waiting while Aminta strains to know what has come.

The chapters move from Cuper's schoolboys to a 'war' at Olmer, the family estate. Old lovers become new friends, and a secret is fished out without angling. Two roads lead toward Steignton as feelings shift and alliances change. Meredith mixes comedy with real feeling in these scenes. The volume tightens the knot between Ormont, Aminta, and Weyburn.
lucian-works-fowler-vol-3:
The Fowler brothers' third volume of Lucian continues their complete English translation of 1905. Lucian's output was huge, and this volume keeps the laughter coming. Imaginary voyages and mock trials of the dead appear among its pieces.

Lucian's jokes preserve a vivid picture of educated belief in the Roman Empire. He parodies historians, tragedians, and religious enthusiasts with a reporter's eye. One famous piece sails to the moon long before science fiction existed. The Fowlers render his Greek into clear, lively Edwardian prose. Satire here doubles as social history of the second century. Few ancient authors entertain while informing this reliably across so many subjects.
lyell-principles-of-geology-vol-3:
Charles Lyell closed his Principles of Geology with a third volume in the early 1830s. After setting out his method, he applied it to the rocks themselves in detail. Water-laid and fire-made causes take center stage in these chapters.

Lyell sorts strata, fossils, and landforms to show gradual change at work. His system made a very old earth, and even ancient human history, seem plausible. Few science books have shifted so many minds at once. The volume completes the founding work of modern geology. Generations of geology students learned the science largely through Lyell's framing of it.
lyra-graeca-edmonds-loeb-vol-3:
Stesichorus, Ibycus, Simonides, and Bacchylides headline the third Loeb volume of Lyra Graeca, in J. M. Edmonds's edition and English version. These poets of the sixth and fifth centuries BCE wrote for cities, kings, and victors across the Greek world. Little of them survives whole, and much came back only from papyrus finds.

Simonides made the epitaph an art and was famed for his memory and his tears for the dead. Bacchylides, his nephew, sang victory odes that rival those of Pindar. Edmonds sets out the fragments with notes on each torn line. The volume completes his gathering of the lyric remains that founded Western song.
madame-chrysantheme-volume-3:
Volume 3 of Madame Chrysanthème was Gutenberg etext number 80. It carries on Pierre Loti's diary of a summer in Japan. The French Academy crowned Loti among its Immortals for such work. His hero is himself, a naval officer far from home.

By this part the Nagasaki season is well advanced. Chrysanthème and her officer husband live their arranged, fragile union. Loti fills pages with processions, music, and harbor scenes. Under the charm runs a note of coming parting. Ships and orders govern a sailor's heart, and his stay must end. The volume lets the reader feel time closing on the summer.
made-to-measure-deep-waters-part-3:
Made to Measure is a comic tale by W. W. Jacobs, from his Deep Waters. This is part three of that collection of short stories. Mr. Mott fetches his niece from the station with great pride. Her photograph had made him nervous about claiming the right girl.

Miss Garland steps down pretty and well dressed, tired of London. She calls his little old town beautiful and peaceful. The lonely old man hopes she will stay a long time. She hints at other things than noise that upset her in town. Jacobs builds his quiet comedy from such small hints. His tales of clerks and watermen are models of dry humor.
mahavastu-senart-vol-3:
The third and last volume of Senart's Mahavastu came out in 1897 and completes his great edition. Le Mahavastu closes here with the last runs of the Buddha legend in Sanskrit. The full work had taken Senart fifteen long years of labor to print.

The closing books bring the long chain of past lives toward the final birth and waking. Kings, gods, and common folk cross the Buddha's path in tale after tale. Senart's finished edition set the standard text for this great Buddhist scripture. Students of early Buddhism still work from his three volumes today.
master-tales-of-mystery-volume-3:
Francis J. Reynolds gathered Master Tales of Mystery, Volume 3. Six tales by Arthur B. Reeve lead the book. They star Craig Kennedy, the famed sleuth of that day.

Reeve's tales name a poisoned pen, a silent bullet, and a steel door. Paul L. Ford adds a great train robbery tale. Max Pemberton, George B. McCutcheon, and Burton E. Stevenson add more. The set mixes crime, fear, and clever proof for fans of short thrills. Joseph Ernest and Marjorie Pickthall close the contents page. Short, sharp cases suit readers who like a puzzle solved in one sitting.
matthew-paris-english-history-giles-vol-:
J. A. Giles's third volume of Matthew Paris runs from 1259 to 1273 and closes the set with the general index to Matthew and to Roger of Wendover. The chronicle that Matthew built at Saint Albans here covers the Barons' War in full. It is the last stretch of the fullest English history of the thirteenth century.

The barons under Simon de Montfort beat the king at Lewes and rule for a year, then fall at Evesham in 1265. Prince Edward rebuilds royal power, and the young Henry's reign ends in 1272. Matthew had died in 1259, and his brothers of Saint Albans carried the tale on. The index opens the whole vast chronicle to the reader.
memoirs-of-extraordinary-popular-delusio:
Volume three of Mackay's Popular Delusions treats learned folly at length. Book one covers the alchemists and their long search. They sought the philosopher's stone and the water of life.

Geber, Avicenna, Albertus Magnus, and Roger Bacon stand in part one. Part two runs through Paracelsus, Dr. Dee, and the Rosicrucians. Count de St. Germain and Cagliostro close that long line of adepts. Book two treats fortune telling, and book three treats the magnetisers. A head on philosophical delusions stands after the magnetisers. Learned men, Mackay shows, can chase folly as hard as crowds.
memoirs-of-henry-hunt-esq-volume-3:
Volume three of Henry Hunt's memoirs opens with a scene of violence. A young woman lay senseless, struck down near a procession. Her scalp wound ran four inches long, the text states.

Blood streamed down her white gown as she came to her senses. Her cap and clothes were torn to rags in the attack. She ran to Hunt and told her wrongs before the crowd. Four to five thousand Bristolians stood by, horror struck at the sight. Hunt says he knows the villain who struck the blow. Outrage drives this volume's start more than self praise.
memoirs-of-madame-la-marquise-de-montesp:
Book three of Madame de Montespan's memoirs opens at chapter thirty five. M. de Lauzun and Mademoiselle de Montpensier head that chapter. The King settles a match, and a secret union follows in the heads.

Mademoiselle falls hard for Lauzun, a man she takes for a lover. She drops her proud reserve and hides her love in glances and signs. At last she hands him a written offer of marriage in a recess. Lauzun feigns awe, sheds tears, and feeds her passion with wiles. The King sends Lauzun to Pignerol in the heads that follow. Gifts from the princess mark her vain hope to free him.
memoirs-of-marguerite-de-valois-queen-of:
Book three of this set holds a History of the House of Valois. The sample names no author for that history in its heads. It starts with Charles, Comte de Valois, brother of Philip the Fair.

When Charles IV's queen bears a daughter, the barons must choose an heir. The peers hold that the crown can pass to no woman, Froissart says. Philip of Valois takes the throne and founds a new royal house. He proves a stern master who strikes the great lords when he can. Edward III's claim, through his mother, is weighed and set aside. Lawyers, the text says, backed the new king against the lords.
merivale-romans-empire-vol-3:
Good emperors rule in the third volume of Merivale's History of the Romans, issued in eighteen sixty-five. Vespasian restores order, and the line runs through Trajan to Marcus Aurelius. Rome enjoys its long golden age of wide peace and wise government under the Flavians and Antonines.

Merivale shows power joined to wisdom across a favored century. Roads, laws, and cities flourish from Britain to Syria in his account. He clearly loves good government and says why it matters. The volume forms the bright center of his work. The Empire stands at its height, ruled for once by wise men.
michel-and-angele-a-ladder-of-swords-vol:
Volume Three closes Gilbert Parker's romance of Michel and Angele amid Elizabethan court intrigue. Its sample chapter studies the Earl of Leicester, the Queen's longtime favorite. Parker describes how Leicester rose by subterranean means, checkmating Spanish, German, and French diplomacy. Yet the same passage condemns the small, scheming habits that built his power.

Parker argues that practiced intriguers lose all sense of proportion. They must scheme even when the stakes are trifling. Against such a court, the Huguenot lovers' fate is decided. The closing volume gives the romance its darkest portrait of power at Elizabeth's court.
milman-history-jews-vol-3:
Maccabees to catastrophe fill the third volume of Milman's History of the Jews, from 1829. The people endure Greek kings, win brief freedom under the Maccabees, then pass under Rome's hard hand. Jerusalem falls in the year 70, the Temple burns, and the dispersion of the Jews begins.

Milman closes his pioneering work with that vast sorrow. He writes the tragedy with restraint, learning, and evident feeling throughout. A clergyman's fairness toward another faith marked the whole enterprise. The three volumes together founded modern Jewish historiography in English, and they still reward readers who want the story told as history, not legend.
mirk-abbey-volume-2-of-3:
James Payn published Mirk Abbey with Hurst and Blackett in London in 1866. This is the second of its three volumes. The volume opens with Lady Lisgard calling her attendant Mary, Mistress Forest, for a serious talk. Mary's respectful tone hides a resolve the narrator marks at once: she has decided to answer no.

Chapter titles promise a confession, a breach of post-office rules, and an uncheerful picnic. The action moves to Epsom and turns on a letter from Paris. Characters named Withers and Arthur Haldane maneuver through thrust and counter-thrust. Payn builds a mid-Victorian tale of secrets, letters, and household power.
mirk-abbey-volume-3-of-3:
The third volume of James Payn's Mirk Abbey, published in London in 1866, closes the three-volume novel. Its chapters introduce Madame de Castellan and a memorial window at the abbey. Titles like Fled, The Uninvited Guest, and Out of the Cage quicken the pace. The volume ends with The Reconciliation, Ralph's Appeal, and Dying Words.

Payn resolves the secrets that Lady Lisgard's household has carried through the earlier volumes. Jacob's guard-ship and a triumphal arch widen the scene beyond the abbey. Three-volume novels like this one supplied the circulating libraries of Victorian England. This final volume delivers the confrontations and settlements its readers awaited.
miscellaneous-writings-and-speeches-volu:
Volume Three of Macaulay's miscellaneous writings turns to his Encyclopaedia Britannica contributions. Five biographical articles anchor the volume. They treat Francis Atterbury, John Bunyan, Oliver Goldsmith, Samuel Johnson, and William Pitt. The dates run from 1853 to 1859, the last years of Macaulay's life.

The volume also gathers his miscellaneous poems and inscriptions. Early pieces include an epitaph on Henry Martyn and lines to Pitt's memory. A Radical War Song and two battle ballads follow, on Moncontour and Naseby. The Naseby poem is credited to a mock Puritan serjeant with an enormous hyphenated name, Macaulay's joke in full view.
mohawks-a-novel-volume-1-of-3:
Mary Elizabeth Braddon's Mohawks appeared in London in 1886, in three volumes. The title page credits only the author of Lady Audley's Secret, Vixen, and Ishmael. John and Robert Maxwell published the novel from Fleet Street. This first volume's chapters carry poetic mottoes as their titles.

The opening chapter is called One That Doth Wear Himself Away in Loneness. The second is A Tedious Road the Weary Wretch Returns. Such headings promise a sensation plot of suffering and endurance. Braddon, the queen of the circulating-library novel, built her three-deckers for readers who wanted a long, tangled story in installments of suspense.
mohawks-a-novel-volume-2-of-3:
Volume Two of Mary Elizabeth Braddon's Mohawks continues the three-volume novel of 1886. John and Robert Maxwell published it in London, as with the first volume. The title page again names its author only by her successes: Lady Audley's Secret, Vixen, and Ishmael. Chapter headings in this volume are also drawn from poetry.

The first chapter here is In Opposition Against Fate and Hell. The second declares, I Stand Upon the Ground of Mine Own Honour. Middle volumes of Victorian three-deckers deepened the knot before the last volume cut it. Braddon's readers expected secrets, threatened honor, and defiance, and these headings promise all three.
mohawks-a-novel-volume-3-of-3:
Volume Three of Mary Elizabeth Braddon's Mohawks closes the London three-volume novel of 1886. John and Robert Maxwell published it, as they did the earlier volumes. Its chapter headings continue the poetic mottoes of the earlier volumes. The first reads, You Called Me, and I Came Home to Your Heart.

The second heading asks, O, To What End, Except a Jealous One? Jealousy and homecoming frame the final movement of Braddon's plot. Last volumes of three-deckers paid off the secrets and sufferings of the first two. Braddon's finale delivers the reckoning her circulating-library readers had waited through two volumes to reach.
monsieur-de-camors-volume-3: The third volume closes Octave Feuillet's Monsieur de Camors in this English edition. The Project Gutenberg header lists it thirty-second in the French Immortals series. Feuillet's society novel ends with its hero's long career reaching its reckoning. The hosted sample, however, preserves no readable content from the volume itself. It contains only the Gutenberg header, with title, author, and series information. Readers learn what the volume is, but see none of its pages.
motley-united-netherlands-vol-3:
Leicester's failed rule fills the third volume of Motley's United Netherlands, from 1869. England's earl governs the Dutch badly, quarreling with the states he came to aid. The Armada years then bind English and Dutch fates together against Spain's great fleet and Philip's vast designs.

Motley braids the two nations' stories with a novelist's skill. Archivist's learning backs every scene of court, camp, and council. England's clumsy help and Dutch grit stand in sharp contrast here. The volume advances his great history toward its close, showing how a small republic learned, at real cost, to stand alone among the great powers of Europe.
mount-royal-a-novel-volume-1-of-3:
Mount Royal, a three-volume novel by the author of Lady Audley's Secret, opened in London in 1882. John and Robert Maxwell published it from Shoe Lane, Fleet Street. The title page withholds Mary Elizabeth Braddon's name, trading on her famous title instead. This first volume's chapters carry motto titles in verse.

The opening chapter is called The Days That Are No More. The second introduces one described as the Lovelace of his day. A Lovelace, in the old novel tradition, is a charming and dangerous rake. Braddon's first volume thus promises lost happiness and a seducer's entrance, the classic machinery of her sensation fiction.
mount-royal-a-novel-volume-2-of-3:
Volume Two of Mount Royal continues Mary Elizabeth Braddon's three-volume novel of 1882. John and Robert Maxwell published it in London, as before. Its chapters continue the motto titles drawn from verse. The first reads, Let Me and My Passionate Love Go By.

The second chapter's motto sighs, Alas for Me Then, My Good Days Are Done. Passion and regret govern this middle volume's weather. In the three-decker form, the second volume deepened entanglements before any rescue. Braddon, identified again only as the author of Lady Audley's Secret, keeps her characters suspended between love and ruin here.
mount-royal-a-novel-volume-3-of-3:
The third volume of Mount Royal closes Mary Elizabeth Braddon's novel of 1882. John and Robert Maxwell of London published the set. Chapter mottoes again head the contents. The first promises, With Such Remorseless Speed Still Come New Woes.

The second chapter is titled Yours on Monday, God's To-day, a motto of sudden death or parting. Final volumes of sensation novels gathered the woes and paid them off. Braddon's readers expected concealed sins to surface and fates to be settled. This volume delivers the conclusion toward which two volumes of mottoes, sighs, and passions have been driving.
mr-crewe-s-career-volume-3:
Volume Three of Winston Churchill's novel contains Book Three, opening with St. Giles of the Blameless Life. The Honourable Adam B. Hunt, the railroads' chosen candidate for governor, smokes on his porch. Bascom, Billings, and Botcher visit to sign expense cheques. Crewe's speech charges that the Northeastern Railroads confer governorships rather than pay for them.

By August the people's campaign is visibly winning. Edmundton and Kingston have more trains and cars, and some rates have already fallen. Reform rallies draw real reporters instead of matinee crowds. Churchill closes his saga with the fight between machine politics and an aroused public at full pitch.
mrs-whittelsey-s-magazine-for-mothers-an:
Mrs. A. G. Whittelsey edited this magazine for mothers and daughters. Volume three came out in New York in 1852. Henry M. Whittelsey published it at 128 Nassau Street. A Bible verse about sons and daughters fronts the volume.

The index lists pieces like A Child's Prayer across hundreds of pages. Such magazines mixed faith, home craft, tales, and advice. They aimed to shape girls into wives and mothers of worth. Mothers were urged to train sons like strong plants. The volume is a full year of one Victorian home journal, a clear window on its readers' hopes and rules.
muqaddimah-prolegomenes-slane-1868-tome-:
The third tome of de Slane's Muqaddimah, published in 1868, completes his French translation of Ibn Khaldun's Prolegomena. Ibn Khaldun devotes this final tome to knowledge itself: the sciences, crafts, and learning of his world. He sorts theology, law, medicine, grammar, poetry, and even dream interpretation and alchemy into one great survey.

His judgments on education remain sharp: how students learn, and how rote teaching fails them. The survey doubles as a portrait of fourteenth-century Islamic civilization from inside. De Slane's three tomes, in the Notices et extraits, fixed the Muqaddimah's European reputation. Historians now rank Ibn Khaldun among the founders of sociology and the philosophy of history. The French text remains a scholarly standard.
nasa-tm-19710010487-msc-apollo-13-invest:
Panel 3 of the Manned Spacecraft Center's Apollo 13 Investigation Team covered flight operations and the tracking network. Addendum 1 to its final report focuses on the lunar module team known as TELMU. It gathers the mission events and consumables figures that the team worked with during and after the flight.

Tables list mission events from before liftoff through the emergency, drawn from team members' logs. A consumables table tracks supplies such as descent oxygen, with early values calculated after the mission and later ones generated in real time. The text examines one odd stretch when descent oxygen use seemed to stop. It links that pause to heat soakback from a descent engine burn and to carbon dioxide building up in the cabin.
nex-pelle-the-conqueror-vol-3:
Pelle steps forward as a labor leader in the third English volume of Nexo's epic. Strikes, meetings, and hard talks with employers fill his days now. The boy who once served on a farm now speaks for men like his father.

Private hopes and public struggle merge as the movement grows across the land. Nexo gives the strikes real weight, with wins, losses, and tired compromises. Pelle's own family life strains under the load of leadership. Few novels of the labor movement match this one for scale and feeling, and this volume is its beating heart.
nicene-post-nicene-fathers-1-vol-3:
Augustine's On the Holy Trinity fills the front of volume three of the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, first series, from 1886. Philip Schaff edited the set. Doctrinal and moral treatises by Augustine fill out the volume behind it.

On the Holy Trinity is Augustine's deepest book: fifteen books seeking the three-in-one God. He finds hints of the Trinity in the mind itself, in its memory, thought, and love. The treatises that follow treat faith, the creed, patience, and the care of the dead. The volume shows Augustine the theologian at full stretch, thinking in Latin for a church that would think with him for a thousand years.
nicene-post-nicene-fathers-2-vol-3:
Volume three of the Nicene Fathers' second series, from 1890, gathers historical writings by Theodoret, Jerome, Gennadius, and Rufinus. Schaff and Wace edited the series. The volume is a shelf of church historians and biographers of scholars.

Theodoret, a Syrian bishop, continues the church's story and writes lives of the desert monks he knew. Jerome's On Illustrious Men is the first dictionary of Christian authors, himself included. Gennadius extends Jerome's list, and Rufinus adds his own continuation of Eusebius. Together they show the early church writing its own memory. Much of what we know of lost writers survives only in these pages.
niebuhr-history-rome-vol-3:
Great crises test Rome in the third volume of Niebuhr's History, in the 1837 Hare and Thirlwall version. The Punic Wars and the republic's fall are rebuilt from the sources. Niebuhr's critical method reaches its full, revolutionary rigor in these chapters on Rome's hardest centuries of war and change.

He taught historians how to read ancient evidence with new eyes. Every claim must show its root in a source he trusts. The book's influence spread far beyond Roman studies into all history writing. Epoch-making in its day, it stays foundational now: the work that proved the past could be reconstructed, not merely retold, by strict and honest method.
night-and-morning-volume-3:
Book the Third of Edward Bulwer Lytton's Night and Morning fills volume three of this copy. A verse from Thomson's Castle of Indolence heads its first chapter. The scene shifts to Paris, in a popular and respectable quarter that is not quite fashionable.

A curious building juts from the shops on the Rue, built like an ancient Roman temple. Green pilasters and gilded cornices dress its front. Three small statues above stand, by rumour, for Hymen, Cupid, and Fortune. A brass plate on the door names Monsieur Love. Lytton sets love, marriage, and luck over a Paris shopfront as his tale resumes.
no-defense-volume-3:
Volume three of Gilbert Parker's No Defense holds Book the Third, which closes the novel. A letter opens the book, then strangers arrive at Salem. Lord Mallow intervenes, and a clash of race follows. Sheila has her say, Noreen comes, and a talk with the governor leads toward what happened.

The first chapter shows a planter at his table on Christmas Day. His lands lie on the Thomas River, a few hours from Spanish Town. He has given presents and kept the feast with his people. A rich table of boar, pigeon pies, and barbecued hog marks the day. Parker sets the close amid plantation life.
normandy-the-scenery-romance-of-its-anci:
Part three of Gordon Home's Normandy opens at chapter seven, concerning Mont St Michel. Verses from Tennyson's Gareth and Lynette head the chapter, about a royal mount flashing through mist. Home quotes an older book on the mount's majestic gulf and its strategic weight in war.

Readers had glimpsed that gulf already from Avranches, in an earlier chapter. Home warns that many miss the rock's best sides by taking the straight national road. The winding coast road from Pontaubault shows more, he says. A tramway now runs along the causeway to the mount itself. Old spell and new ease meet at the famous rock.
northern-lights-volume-3:
Volume three of Gilbert Parker's Northern Lights holds When the Swallows Homeward Fly, George's Wife, and Marcile. The first tale opens as the sun stalks away into evening. Banners of gold and crimson trail behind it, and swift twilight streams over the land. Two men on a high hill watch it go.

One man's look is like a light in a window to a lost traveller. He has made a journey few attempt and fewer finish. On foot and alone, save for dogs and Indian guides, he reached the far northwestern Arctic seas. Ice hummocks housed him, and pemmican and seal fat fed him. Parker honours endurance in the far North.
one-of-our-conquerors-volume-3:
George Meredith's third volume opens with book three. Chapter nineteen pits Nature against Circumstance in men's hearts. Active men feel the two forces split apart, he writes. Soldiers and heroes know that wild moment well, he says. They march on while praising Nature's topping wisdom.

A great assembly at Lakelands follows in chapter twenty. Dartrey Fenellan and an intruder named Jarniman enter. A ladies' lapdog causes momentous effects from minor causes. Nesta's engagement closes this part of the novel. Meredith blends satire, romance, and moral debate. The balance of nature and duty is his lasting theme.
orderic-vitalis-ecclesiastical-history-f:
Thomas Forester's third volume of the Ecclesiastical History of Orderic Vitalis came out in 1855. Orderic wrote at Saint Evroul in Normandy, an English-born monk watching two kingdoms at once. His history is the fullest Norman chronicle of his century.

Crusaders' tales from the Holy Land, the wars of Henry I, and the affairs of Norman churches and courts fill this stretch of the work. Orderic gathers reports from returning knights and pilgrims, and he marks marvels beside hard fact. His cast runs from kings to hermits and robber saints. Readers who want the feel of the Anglo-Norman world, not just its wars, come to Orderic.
pahlavi-texts-west-vol-3:
West's third volume of Pahlavi Texts appeared in 1885 in the Sacred Books of the East. He continued rescuing Zoroastrian literature from Middle Persian originals. Priestly writings from Persia under Islamic rule fill the volume.

The contents include the Sad Dar, a popular summary of religious duties. Other pieces offer hymns, legends, and moral counsel for the faithful. Such writings kept an endangered tradition alive across hard centuries. West translated with patience and supplied full scholarly notes. His five-volume project remains a monument of preservation. Readers meet Zoroastrianism here as a living community's faith. The tradition's refusal to disappear gives these pages their quiet power.
palfrey-history-new-england-vol-3:
John Gorham Palfrey's History of New England reached Volume 3 in 1858. The founding fathers give way here to their children and heirs. A second generation takes up the Puritan errand in the wilderness.

Churches, schools, and town meetings fill the middle movement of the work. Sons are tested against the high vision their fathers brought over. Faith cools for some, while towns grow rich and sure of themselves. Palfrey writes as a proud heir of the people he studies. The volume shows a holy mission hardening into a settled, lasting society over time. Strain between old ideals and new habits runs through it.
pappus-collection-hultsch-vol-3:
Friedrich Hultsch finished his edition of Pappus of Alexandria in 1878 with this third volume. It holds the fragments of book eight of the Mathematical Collection, on mechanics, with supplements and full indexes. The Greek text comes with Hultsch's Latin version. Pappus wrote around 320 CE.

Book eight treats centers of gravity, inclined planes, and the machines of the engineer. Even in scraps it shows Greek mechanics at its most exact. The indexes open the whole Collection to study, name by name and term by term. With this volume the richest source for lost Greek geometry stands complete in its classic edition. No public domain English version exists.
pausanias-description-greece-frazer-vol-:
Frazer's third Pausanias volume carries the commentary south into the Peloponnese. Pausanias's route runs through Sparta, Olympia, and Argos in this section. Frazer's 1898 edition matches the traveler against the landscape itself.

Olympia's games and statues receive especially full archaeological treatment. Spartan customs and Argive legends get tested against stones and inscriptions. Frazer sets each legend against its landscape with tireless learning. His method shows readers how to verify an ancient author. The old heartland of Greek myth becomes a mapped, walkable country. Scholars still consult these volumes when excavating the sites Pausanias described two millennia ago.
pentagon-papers-vol-3:
The Pentagon Papers were a classified history of the Vietnam War written inside the Defense Department in the late 1960s. Volume 3 of the Senator Gravel edition, issued in 1971, covers the years when the United States took over the fighting. Gravel's edition put the leaked record before any reader who wanted it.

These pages hold the memos, cables, and studies behind the bombing campaigns and the huge troop build-up of 1965 to 1968. They show leaders weighing wider war against the risk of Chinese or Soviet entry, and doubting their own strategy as casualties rose. Read beside the era's public statements, the volume documents the gap between what officials said and what they believed.
personal-memoirs-of-p-h-sheridan-volume-:
Part 3 of volume 1 of Sheridan's memoirs opens at Chattanooga in September 1863, just after Chickamauga. His troops take position inside the entrenchments while the enemy fortifies Lookout Mountain and Missionary Ridge. The army sits in partial siege, its supplies dragged sixty miles over mountain roads from Bridgeport.

Sheridan describes headquarters under the shadow of Lookout Mountain, shells dropping into camp, and the loyal Mr. Crutchfield feeding him information. The chapter builds toward Grant's arrival and the battles for the heights. It shows Sheridan waiting, exposed and shelled, on the eve of his famous charge up Missionary Ridge.
personal-memoirs-of-u-s-grant-part-3:
Part 3 of Grant's memoirs opens at chapter twenty-seven, in 1862, with Grant chafing at Corinth. He holds a nominal command and yet no command under Halleck, and asks again and again to be relieved. Sherman calls as he is packing and urges him so strongly not to go that he stays.

Granted removal of his headquarters to Memphis, Grant rides west with a tiny escort through unguarded country. He dines at La Grange with a secessionist host who proudly feeds soldiers' families from his plantations. Grant listens, and files the man away. The part shows a general waiting for his chance.
pierre-and-his-people-tales-of-the-far-n:
Volume 3 of Gilbert Parker's Pierre and His People collects four far north tales: Shon McGann's Tobogan Ride, Pere Champagne, The Scarlet Hunter, and The Stone. Pretty Pierre, the figure who links the whole set, moves through a world of mountain huts, buffalo robes, and Hudson's Bay men.

Shon McGann's Tobogan Ride opens in a mountain hut, where Shon sings of Farcalladen Rise with his pipe between his teeth. Around him sit Pretty Pierre, Jo Gordineer, the Honourable Just Trafford, and their host Prince Levis, a French Canadian whose princely name was a Rocky Mountain joke. Talk turns to the ghost of Guidon Mountain while a drink called ginger-tea is made under the eye of prohibition law.
plato-dialogues-jowett-vol-3:
Benjamin Jowett's third volume of Plato holds three works, and the first of them is the giant: the Republic. In ten books, Socrates and his friends build a just city in speech to learn what justice is in a single soul. The volume's other works reach even higher.

The Republic gives Plato's theory of the ideal state, ruled by philosopher kings, and his allegory of the cave. Timaeus then tells how a divine craftsman shaped the cosmos, and Critias begins the tale of Atlantis and its war with ancient Athens. No other volume of Plato has shaped Western thought more. Jowett's translation keeps its Victorian polish.
poems-volume-3: The third volume of Meredith's poems, continuing his exploration of man's place in nature and society. "The Woods of Westermain" and other sequences show his cosmic optimism in full flow. Challenging verse from one of the Victorian age's most independent minds.
pretiosa-margarita-novella-de-thesavro-a: Pretiosa margarita novella, third copy, 1546. The precious pearl. This book preserves that work. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
prince-zilah-volume-3: The third volume of Prince Zilah brings the romance to its climax. Long-buried secrets of the hero's past come to light. Stern honor demands its painful sacrifice. A stirring close to a popular novel.
quintilian-institutio-butler-loeb-vol-3:
The third Loeb volume of Quintilian's Institutio Oratoria, in H. E. Butler's English, holds books six through eight. The Roman teacher's great course on speaking now turns from the bones of a case to its life. Style, feeling, and the handling of a jury come to the front.

Book six treats the closing appeal, the rousing of pity and anger, and the use of laughter. Book seven orders the arguments, and book eight opens the study of style: clarity, ornament, and tropes. Quintilian quotes poets and orators on every page to make his points live. These books show rhetoric as an art of moving minds.
ranke-history-england-vol-3:
Volume 3 of Ranke's History, in the 1875 Oxenford translation, swings with England's faith. The boy king Edward rules first, then Mary drives a Catholic return. Elizabeth's early years close the book's span of fierce change.

Each reign reverses the last one's church settlement in turn. Ranke follows the swings with his usual depth and calm control. He shows how faith, fear, and foreign threats shaped each choice. Protestants burn under Mary, then Catholics suffer under her sister. The nation's soul seems at stake in every parliament and pulpit. Ranke gives the struggle the weight of great European history.
ranke-reformation-germany-vol-3:
Volume 3 of Ranke's German Reformation history appeared in Austin's version in 1844. The Schmalkaldic War tests the new faith by force of arms. The Peace of Augsburg then secures it by treaty and law.

Ranke closes with the famed rule that ends the long struggle. Each prince's faith, the treaty says, shall be his land's faith. That harsh bargain shaped Germany for a hundred years to come. Dissenters must yield, move, or hide under the new settlement's terms. Ranke judges the deal with his master's calm and distance. The volume ends an age and explains the map it left.
reymont-the-peasants-vol-3:
Spring wakes the land in the third English volume of Reymont's The Peasants. Fields thaw, work resumes, and passions rise with the sap in the trees. The struggle for land, the peasant's endless obsession, pushes the Boryna drama toward open tragedy.

Lust, jealousy, and pride break through the village's strict customs. Reymont matches the season's surge of life with rising heat in his tale. Every planting and festival carries a charge of hope or menace. Many readers find this the most intense of the four volumes, where the great Polish village saga presses hardest on its people.
sacred-books-east-vol-20-vinaya-texts-3:
Volume twenty of the Sacred Books of the East closes the Vinaya Texts with the Cullavagga, in the 1885 translation by T. W. Rhys Davids and Hermann Oldenberg. The Cullavagga, the Lesser Series, finishes the Pali rule book for monks and nuns. Parts one and two stand in volumes thirteen and seventeen.

The Cullavagga rules daily life in fine grain: dwellings, furniture, bathing, and the duties of teacher and pupil. It also tells of the first council after the Buddha's death, where the teaching was recited and fixed. The founding of the order of nuns appears here too. With it, the Vinaya set stands complete in English.
satapatha-brahmana-eggeling-vol-3:
Eggeling's third volume of the Satapatha Brahmana appeared in 1894. The Sacred Books of the East series carried it as volume forty-one. Creation stories and a great flood legend appear within its ritual exposition.

Later Indian epics would retell several myths preserved in these books. Readers meet the gods as working priests knew them, inside sacrifice itself. The volume shows myth living inside ritual rather than in storybooks. Eggeling's notes guide readers through the dense ceremonial detail. Ancient India's imagination survives here in prose of great age. The flood tale of Manu, ancestor of humanity, is among its treasures for comparative mythology.
sherman-memoirs-vol-2-part-3:
Part Three of Sherman's memoirs, in Volume Two, covers his most famous campaign: the March to the Sea. In late 1864 Sherman cut loose from Atlanta and marched across Georgia to Savannah. His 1875 account tells it as he planned it.

Sherman explains why he tore up rails, lived off the land, and aimed at the South's will to fight. The Carolinas campaign follows, harder and wetter than Georgia. His memoirs defend the march as humane in the long run, since it shortened the war. Critics in the South never agreed, and the argument still runs. His men called the march bumming, and Sherman does not hide the foraging.
strabo-geography-hamilton-falconer-vol-3:
Volume Three of Strabo's Geography, in the Hamilton and Falconer version, holds Books Fourteen through Seventeen. The survey moves east and south to finish the known world. Asia, Egypt, and Libya close the great tour.

Strabo describes ports, rivers, and peoples at the edge of Roman rule. Egypt gets a long, rich account of its land and temples. His sources thin out here, and wonders grow more common. The volume completes a work of vast scope. With it, readers hold the fullest picture the ancient world ever drew of itself.
stubbs-constitutional-history-vol-3:
Volume 3 of Stubbs's Constitutional History of England appeared in 1878. The Tudor age transforms the old order across this final book. Henry's break with Rome and his Reformation Parliament lead the change.

Royal supremacy over the church bends the old constitution to new ends. Stubbs shows how medieval forms survived while their meaning shifted fast. Councils, courts, and parliaments serve a stronger, more central crown. His three volumes close with the modern state coming into view. Generations learned from Stubbs where England's freedoms first took root. The work's scale and care have kept it in print ever since.
symonds-renaissance-italy-vol-3:
Fine arts fill Volume 3 of Symonds's Renaissance in Italy, from 1875. Painters, sculptors, and builders from Giotto to Michelangelo pass in review. Churches, palaces, and frescoed halls rise across his glowing chapters.

Symonds writes of pictures and buildings with rare grace and feeling. His lives of the great artists rank among the finest in English. He shows how patrons, cities, and rival masters drove art upward. Technique serves beauty, and beauty serves civic pride in his tale. Readers gain a full map of the age's visual glory here. Prose worthy of its subject carries the whole splendid survey.
tales-from-the-arabic-payne-1884-vol-3:
Payne's Tales from the Arabic closes with Volume III, printed in 1884 alongside the end of his Nights. The last Breslau and Calcutta stories take their place in English, in the translator's full and faithful style. With this volume, John Payne's double project stands whole: the great cycle and its overflow, both complete.

The supplement's tales reward the reader who wants more of the world the Nights opened. Their plots turn on wit, luck, and the thin line between beggar and king. Volume III finishes a set that scholars use to trace how Arabic story collections grew beyond any single book.
talleyrand-memoirs-vol-3:
In Volume Three, Talleyrand tells of Napoleon's fall and the Bourbon Restoration that followed. The French diplomat had bet against his old master and helped shape what came next. Beaufort's translation keeps his dry voice intact.

The volume covers the collapse of the Empire, the return of the Bourbon kings, and France's uneasy peace. Talleyrand defends his dealings with the allies and his role at the settlement of Europe. Old scores are settled in smooth, polite prose. For students of diplomacy, this is a master class in surviving defeat. Paris crowds, allied armies, and a nervous court crowd these chapters.
the-adventures-of-tom-sawyer-part-3: The trial of Muff Potter brings Tom's conscience to the fore in this third part — will he speak and face Injun Joe? Twain's courtroom drama grips like a thriller. Moral courage meets boyish fear. Tom's trembling testimony saves an innocent man and seals his own danger.
the-complete-writings-of-charles-dudley-: Volume three of Warner's complete writings: travel, humor, and reflection. The complete Hartford circle in one author. Warm and readable throughout. Warner's third volume continues the pleasant journey, travel and reflection in good company, in good company throughout.
the-confession-of-a-child-of-the-century: The third volume of Musset's Confession deepens the young man's despair. Love proves as hollow and cold as pleasure. The romantic malaise reaches its darkest depth. A despairing cry from a brilliant and lost generation.
the-confessions-of-harry-lorrequer-volum: The Confessions of Harry Lorrequer, volume three, by Charles Lever. The Irish soldier's tales continue. This book preserves that novel. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
the-diary-and-letters-of-madame-d-arblay: The Diary and Letters of Madame D'Arblay, volume three. Fanny Burney's journals continue. This book preserves that memoir. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Scholars prize such firsthand sources from long ago.
the-dwelling-place-of-light-volume-3: The third volume carries Churchill's industrial novel toward its powerful close. Strikes, love, and moral reckoning intertwine in the mill town. The characters face the full costs of their hardest choices. A thoughtful and satisfying end to a serious story.
the-forsyte-saga-volume-3: The last volume of the Forsyte Saga: old Jolyon's line fades as England changes. Soames grows old, and the new age has little use for Forsytes. Galsworthy's elegy for a class and a century, tender and just.
the-french-revolution-volume-3: Taine brings his great history of the Revolution to its close in this third volume. The Terror passes, the Directory fails, and Napoleon looms. His stern verdict on the whole upheaval has shaped debate ever since. A mighty and somber finale.
the-great-conspiracy-volume-3: The third volume carries the war through 1862 — Shiloh, Antietam, and the Emancipation Proclamation. Logan writes as both soldier and statesman, never doubting the Union cause. Stirring history from one who helped make it. From the Peninsula to Antietam's cornfield, Logan follows the armies with a soldier's eye and a patriot's heart.
the-home-book-of-verse-volume-3: Volume three of the Home Book of Verse: more of English poetry's treasures. Stevenson's taste never falters through the vast collection. The anthology continues in glory. The third volume is as rich as the first.
the-legends-of-the-jews-volume-3: Ginzberg’s third book holds more old tales of the sages. Wonders fill page after page of this rich and loving lore. A treasure for all who love the old stories, gathered with care and devotion.
the-prince-and-the-pauper-part-3: Tom plays the prince while Edward learns the pauper's hard lessons in these middle chapters. Twain's satire of courts and slums bites ever deeper. The switched lives grow more perilous and more funny. Each new scrape teaches the boys what pomp and poverty truly mean.
the-purcell-papers-volume-3: Sheridan Le Fanu's Purcell Papers (1880) gathers Irish ghost stories chillingly. The dead walk softly at night. The Tower library holds the full complete text. It papers Purcell eerily and well. Dublin haunts these dark tales. Ghosts whisper warnings clearly. Readers shivered with delight.
the-works-of-edgar-allan-poe-volume-3: Volume three of Poe's works: tales of mystery and imagination from America's dark genius. "The Fall of the House of Usher" and its kin show his power undimmed. Essential for every lover of the strange.
the-writings-of-samuel-adams-volume-3: Volume three of Samuel Adams's writings: more letters and papers from the Revolution's engine room. His political mind works on every page, turning anger into action. The founding's essential documents, in the hand of its fiercest organizer.
their-silver-wedding-journey-volume-3: Howells's Silver Wedding Journey, volume three: the European tour's close. The Marches come home. The dean's gentle art. A travel classic, the Marches come home, the tour's close, gentle art, home again, Howells, the close.
thirlwall-history-greece-vol-3:
Persia's great invasion fills Volume 3 of Thirlwall's History, from 1845. Marathon, Thermopylae, and Salamis stand as the book's famed set pieces. Small Greek cities face the vast empire of the Great King.

Thirlwall tells the heroic age with a scholar's care for proof. He praises courage without inflating it past what sources allow him. Athens and Sparta, rivals at home, stand as one against Persia. The wins that saved Greek freedom get neither bombast nor cold doubt. His warmth stays quiet, his facts stay firm, page by page. The volume remains a model of how to write patriotic history honestly.
to-win-the-love-he-sought-the-great-awak: To Win the Love He Sought, volume three of The Great Awakening. The romance concludes. This book preserves that story. The paper lived through the years. It waits for future eyes. Time has kept the file intact.
un-ga-res-3:
War criminals still at large haunted the victors of the Second World War. Resolution 3 of the General Assembly was passed on 13 February 1946. It recalls the Moscow Declaration of 1943. In it, Roosevelt, Stalin, and Churchill had pledged that enemy crimes would be judged. It also cites the war crimes terms of the Nuremberg Charter of August 1945. Some guilty men, the text says, still dodge justice in the lands of some states.

Member states are urged to act at once. They should arrest the war criminals who bore blame for these crimes, or who took a consenting part in them. The men are to be sent back to the lands where their deeds were done, to be judged and punished under the laws of those lands.
un-ga-res-a-69-3: West Africa's Ebola outbreak forced the UN to build an emergency mission in 2014, and Resolution A/69/3 deals with its budget. The Assembly had read the Secretary-General's report on the United Nations Mission for Ebola Emergency Response. The report also covered the Office of the Special Envoy on Ebola. It takes note of the report and backs the views of its budget advisers, with a warning that the vote settles nothing about the mission's shape or staffing for good.
un-ga-res-es-11-3:
Russia lost its seat on the UN Human Rights Council under Resolution ES-11/3, passed by the General Assembly in emergency session in April 2022. The text recalls the 2006 rule that set up the council. Under it, the Assembly may suspend a member that commits gross and steady breaches of human rights. Grave reports from Ukraine, under Russian attack since February 2022, fill the grounds.

The Council itself had voiced grave concern in March 2022 at reports of such breaches by Russian forces. The Assembly cites its own March votes on the war, then acts: Russia's rights of membership in the council are suspended. Few states have ever drawn that penalty.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 3, adopted on 13 February 1946, called for the arrest and return of war criminals. The Assembly cited the Moscow Declaration of 1943 on enemy cruelty. It cited the laws of war in the Hague Convention of 1907. It cited the war crimes definitions in the charter of the International Military Tribunal. It held that some offenders were still dodging justice in certain lands.

Members were urged to act at once to arrest those who had ordered or willingly joined in such crimes. They were urged to send them back to the countries where the deeds were done. There they were to be tried and punished under those countries' laws. Governments outside the United Nations were called on to do the same.

Resolution 69/3 of the General Assembly is a short budgetary note on the United Nations Mission for Ebola Emergency Response, the emergency mission created during the 2014 West African outbreak. The Assembly acts on the Secretary-General's report and the advice of its Advisory Committee on Administrative and Budgetary Questions. It takes note of the report and endorses the Advisory Committee's conclusions. It stresses that this step does not prejudge its later review of the mission's budget, structure, staffing, and operations. That review comes once a detailed budget is submitted.

UN General Assembly Resolution ES-11/3 — the 2022 emergency-session resolution suspending Russia from the Human Rights Council. It punished Moscow over Ukraine atrocities. The 2022 Council suspension is the Moscow punishment: the Russian Council membership formally revoked over Ukraine atrocities here.
un-sc-res-3:
Security Council Resolution 3 dealt with the Iranian crisis of 1946, one of the first disputes the young council faced. The catalog year of 1942 predates the UN itself and is wrong. Iran had charged that Soviet troops stayed on its soil past the agreed date for leaving after the war, and Tehran brought the complaint to the council in New York.

The resolution noted talks between Iran and the Soviet Union and asked both sides to report back on their progress. It kept the matter on the council's list in case talks failed. Soviet forces withdrew that spring. The case showed both the promise and the limits of the new body's reach.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci: UN Security Council Resolution 3 — the 1946 resolution addressing Soviet troops remaining in Iran after World War II. It was among the very first crises the new Security Council ever handled. The 1946 Iran crisis is the first: the new Council’s earliest handled disputes.
uncle-robert-s-geography-uncle-robert-s-: Educator Francis Wayland Parker believed children learn geography best through stories, and this book proves it. Uncle Robert takes his young visitors on imagined journeys across the country, turning maps into adventures. Part of a beloved series, it taught generations of schoolchildren to see the wider world with curious eyes.
vedanta-sutras-thibaut-vol-3:
Thibaut completed his Vedanta Sutras translation with a third volume in 1904. It appeared as volume forty-eight of the Sacred Books of the East. The volume finishes Ramanuja's commentary on Badarayana's aphorisms in English.

With both great commentaries now fully translated, readers could compare the systems whole. Sankara's non-dualism and Ramanuja's qualified monism stand side by side. Thibaut's own introductions judge between the rivals with scholarly care. The set became a landmark of English Indology on publication. Later translators refined details, but Thibaut's architecture endured. Anyone studying Vedanta seriously still reckons with his three volumes and their arrangement.
vyse-operations-gizeh-vol-3:
Volume Three of Howard Vyse's Operations serves as the appendix to his Gizeh work. It gathers the papers, letters, and plates that back the main journals. The volume appeared in 1842, after the dig ended.

Findings are set out with lists, notes, and views of the sites. Other scholars' letters weigh in on the results. The plates show chambers and objects as the team found them. Thorough readers get the proof behind the story here. The set closes a record that, for all its flaws, still anchors study of the pyramids.
wanda-vol-1-of-3: Wanda, volume one of three, by Ouida. The opening of the tale. This book preserves that Victorian novel. It holds its historical place. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
wanda-vol-2-of-3: Wanda, volume two of three, by Ouida. The middle of the Polish countess's tale. This book preserves that Victorian novel. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
wanda-vol-3-of-3: Wanda, volume three of three, by Ouida. The close of the tale. This book preserves that Victorian novel. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
yoga-vasistha-mitra-vol-3:
The third volume of Mitra's Yoga-Vasistha continues the immense dialogue between the sage Vasistha and Prince Rama. Vihari-Lala Mitra issued his four-volume English version in the 1890s. By this stage the teaching has moved from the world's unreality to the state of the liberated soul.

Vasistha describes the man who is free while living: calm in gain and loss, acting without bondage to the act. More tales unfold, of worlds nested in atoms and lives relived in dream. The doctrine is radical idealism: consciousness alone is real, and all else its play. The volume holds the epic's most sustained philosophy. Mitra's notes help readers through the Sanskrit terms.
zibeline-volume-3: The third volume of Zibeline carries the story toward its close. Long-hidden motives surface darkly as the end approaches. The elegant world trembles on its foundations. A satisfying French finale, elegant to the very last.
